posts.text: Denny Adan Gonzalez, a 33-year-old man from Cuba, died on April 28 at Stewart Detention Center in Lumpkin, Georgia in a suspected suicide. He is the 18th person to die in ICE custody in 2026, and the 48th since January 2025.

Gonzalez is the fourth Cuban national to die in ICE custody since January 2025. Two of those four deaths occurred in the last sixteen days. Andrew Free's Detention Kills newsletter broke this one first, worth following if you track this issue.

DetentionReports.com, the site Adam Sawyer and I built at Relevant Research to track ICE's detention population in near-real time, just received a major redesign. Here's what changed and why it matters as the detained population keeps growing.

The site has been cited by The Guardian, L.A. Times, PBS, HuffPost, CalMatters, and many others, across the political spectrum. If you're reporting on detention or want to understand what's happening in a facility near you, it's the right place to start.

The dataset has real limitations the authors acknowledge: county policies are mostly absent, the study ends in 2021, and the second Trump administration's wave of enforcement legislation isn't captured yet. That's exactly the gap that makes extending this data urgent.

Three anti-sanctuary states used financial penalties to prevent localities from enacting sanctuary policies. That mechanism ( threatening local budgets to enforce state policy) is becoming more common under the current administration.

Most local sanctuary ordinances (21 of 24) were passed during the first Trump administration. Most state anti-sanctuary laws were passed during the Obama years. States appear to act as a check on the federal government, whichever party holds it.

The geographic pattern is sharp. Anti-sanctuary laws were concentrated in the South, with 17 of 27 enacted there. Sanctuary laws concentrated in the West. Local sanctuary ordinances skewed Northeast; 15 of 24 city ordinances were in Northeastern cities.

The Drexel team identified 340 total policies(288 local and 52 state) enacted over that period. By 2021, more than half of all U.S. states had enacted either a sanctuary or an anti-sanctuary law. That's a significant shift in the legal landscape in roughly one decade.

A new pre-proof in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine does something that's been needed for a long time: a systematic legal mapping of sanctuary and anti-sanctuary policies across all 50 states and hundreds of localities from 2000 to 2021. Worth reading carefully.

Understanding what data exists and how to get it matters more right now than at any point I can remember. The ACoM piece is a useful primer for anyone covering enforcement at the local level.

The broader point: contracts, MOUs, oversight documents, and law enforcement records are producible. Local collaboration with ICE is rarely invisible, it leaves a paper trail if you know where to look and are willing to be persistent about getting it.

The First Amendment Coalition, representing immigrant rights nonprofit Buen Vecino, filed suit and won. The county released the public records, including roughly ten hours of body camera footage. That's how public records law is supposed to work.

In Ventura County last July, sheriff's deputies joined a federal immigration operation at a farm. One farmworker died. At least 361 migrants were arrested. The county initially refused to release records explaining why local law enforcement was there.

American Community Media covered a briefing last week on how journalists and the public can track local immigration enforcement and I was glad to be part of the conversation. The Ventura County case they open with is worth understanding in detail.

Stewart is the largest ICE detention facility in the country right now, according to current data from detentionreports.com. It holds 1,752 beds, is run by #CoreCivic in rural Georgia (140 miles from Atlanta) and has been the subject of sustained scrutiny for years.

The geography matters here. Four of the 48 deaths since January 2025 have occurred in Georgia. Florida and Texas account for nine each. Together, those three states account for nearly half of all in-custody deaths under the current administration.

Jan. 1 through April 28 is 117 days. 18 deaths over 117 days is one death every 6.5 days. At that pace, ICE will report roughly 56 deaths by year's end. For context, 2025 was already the deadliest year for ICE detention in more than two decades, with 32.
